name: Duhumbi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_locator: (Zenodo record 1284478, Description field, 2018-06-06); supporting: p. 2, section 'CONSTRICTED SYLLABLES ALWAYS UNSTRESSED'; Brill 2020 sec. 2.6 refinements only as Google Books excerpts (q3, q14, q16, q20).
catalog_quote: In Duhumbi, stress in general is non-distinctive, prosodic, and relatively unpronounced. In both disyllabic and polysyllabic words, stress falls on the first syllable. This also holds for polymorphemic lexemes, such as inflected words with suffixes. In glossary items in the Duhumbi lexicon, stress is indicated by a stress mark [ˈ] before the stressed syllable, whenever it is not predictable. Phrase stress is generally initial and falling towards the end of the phrase, ... || Most morphemes that feature a constricted syllable are the second syllable in a morphological word, be it either a root preceded by a prefix, the second syllable of a polysyllabic word, or a modifying marker that is preceded by a noun or verb root. In other words, in Duhumbi, as a language with a trochaic foot, these are the unstressed syllables of the word. There are only a few known examples where the constricted syllable receives the primary stress: prefixes followed by a marker or a prefix followed by a root will always receive stress, and the present marker -deʔ ~ -teʔ PRES, the non-past subjunctive -tʰeʔ SUBJ:NPST also receive stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is weak and non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of di- and polysyllabic words (trochaic foot), including on a prefix when one is present and in suffixed/inflected words. The Brill 2020 sec. 2.6 intro (snippet) refines this: in nominal parts of speech stress is generally initial whether or not the first syllable is a prefix; in verbal parts of speech the root is generally stressed and bound morphemes (prefixes and suffixes) unstressed, negation prefixes and case markers never stressed, a few suffixes (present -deʔ~-teʔ, non-past subjunctive -tʰeʔ) do take stress; lexically unpredictable cases are marked with [ˈ] in the lexicon.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No general rule stated in the open texts; a Brill 2020 snippet mentions 'secondary stress on the nominaliser' in one transcribed example ([ˌat'da:ɕiba:le]-type), nothing systematic seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'whenever it is not predictable' is marked in the lexicon (so some lexical exceptions exist); polysyllabic nominal forms where a non-first syllable is stressed are said to exist (snippet); verbal words: root stressed, negation prefixes and case markers never stressed; present -deʔ~-teʔ and subjunctive -tʰeʔ receive stress (zenodo.1284482); many Bodish/Tshangla loans.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (lexemes incl. inflected words); phrase stress separately described as initial and falling. Stress described as phonetically weak ('relatively unpronounced'); language non-tonal with incipient glottalisation-linked pitch contrasts (zenodo.1284476).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Duhumbi as spoken in the Chug valley (Duhum etc.), West Kameng, i.e. exactly chug1252/cvg. Bodt notes the sister variety Khispi (Lish, lish1235? = 'Lishpa') shares the trochaic pattern, while Sartang/Sherdukpen (other Western Kho-Bwa) are iambic; that Khispi remark is incidental and not a description of Khispi.

tone_statements.citation: Bodt, Timotheus Adrianus. 2024. Proto-Western Kho-Bwa: Reconstructing a community's past through language (Language and Linguistics Monograph Series 67). Taipei: Institute of Linguistics, Academia Sinica. xviii+804 pp. [822-page PDF]. ISBN 978-626-7341-64-3 (PDF). Ch. III 'Phonological inventories', sec. 3.1 'Duhumbi' (pp. 58-62); ch. IV 'Phonotactics', sec. 4.2 'Iambic versus trochaic rhythm' (pp. 156-157) and sec. 4.4.1 'Phonological reduction of prefixes' (p. 170).
tone_statements.quote: In addition, most Duhumbi speakers make a distinction between longer, level, open vowels [aː, e, iː, ɔː, u] and shorter, glottal constricted, creaky, high-rising pitched variants [á̰ˀ, ḛ́ˀ, íˀ, ɔ̰́ˀ, ṵ́ˀ]. || Khispi and Duhumbi have trochaic rhythm with stress on the first syllable of a word, and thus even stress prefixes, which is why prefixes maintained their full CiV(Cf) syllabic shape.
tone_statements.locator: p. 58, ch. III sec. 3.1.1 'Duhumbi vowels' (first passage); p. 170, ch. IV sec. 4.4.1 'Phonological reduction of prefixes' (second passage); see also sec. 4.2 'Iambic versus trochaic rhythm', p. 156
tone_statements.summary: No independent lexical tone system is posited: high-rising pitch (with creak and shortness) is a concomitant of the glottal-constricted vowels /aˀ eˀ iˀ oˀ uˀ/ contrasting with long level-pitch modal vowels, i.e. a marginal glottalisation-conditioned pitch contrast; word stress trochaic (first syllable, prefixes included).

tone_statements.citation: Bodt, Timotheus Adrianus. 2018. Duhumbi Phonology - Pitch and Tone. Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1284476 (PDF 'Pitch and Tone').
tone_statements.quote: Strictly speaking, according to these results, a distinctive level tone versus high rising-falling tonal contrast on the vowel /a/ for onsets starting with the nasals /m, n/ and the approximants /y, l/ (but not for w or r) needs to be posited for Duhumbi. However, as Table 2 indicates, most of these lexemes have Bodish cognates [...]. This suggests that a tonal difference in these lexemes is not a native Duhumbi phenomenon, but rather a borrowed phonological feature. Though not an absent feature, tone in Duhumbi carries a low functional load and is in the process of developing itself under influence of contact languages, rather than a native distinctive feature.

sources.citation: Bodt, Timotheus Adrianus. 2018. Duhumbi Phonology - Iambic to Trochaic Rhythm? Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1284482 (4-page PDF 'From iambic to trochaic rhythm').
sources.note: Duhumbi has a trochaic foot: constricted (second) syllables are the unstressed syllables of the word; 'prefixes followed by a marker or a prefix followed by a root will always receive stress', present -deʔ~-teʔ and subjunctive -tʰeʔ also receive stress; stress shifted historically from root (PWKB iambic, as still in Sartang/Sherdukpen) to the initial syllable/prefix; transcriptions like [ˈkʰɔː-lɔk̚] 'head', [ˈmɛm-pʰɔŋ] 'cucumber'.

tone.says: Duhumbi is treated as a non-tonal language in which pitch is largely predictable: plosive-coda and glottal-constricted rhymes carry an inherent rising-falling pitch (no onset-conditioned contrast there); plosive, fricative and affricate onsets show high-falling vs low-level pitch co-varying with voicing/aspiration; only on /a/-syllables with nasal /m, n/ and approximant /y, l/ onsets do a handful of (near-)minimal pairs force a level vs high rising-falling contrast, and these 'high' items are m…
